episode.lensDescription: Examine complexity and tradeoffs. Surface the questions worth asking.
episode.broadcastScript:
Welcome to The Innovation Pulse from Innovating Higher Ed. It's Monday, March 9th, 2026.

When students start demanding to know which professors use A.I. in their courses, institutions face questions they weren't prepared to answer. At the University of Missouri, a student group is pushing for transparency that's driving policy changes campus-wide. We'll explore what this means for academic freedom and pedagogical choice.

-

First, let's catch up on three other stories making waves in higher ed this week.

-

In our Insights and Trends category, N.P.R. reports that colleges remain deeply divided on A.I. use in coursework. Some educators compare using A.I. for writing assignments to bringing a forklift to the gym, while others view it as a valuable learning tool when used responsibly. About 85 percent of students now use A.I. for coursework, but many experience conflicted feelings about outsourcing their thinking. The disconnect between student and faculty approaches is creating friction on campuses nationwide.

-

From our Ethical A.I. file, the Conference on College Composition and Communication has passed a resolution affirming students' and faculty's right to decline generative A.I. in writing classrooms. The resolution cites concerns about data privacy, labor rights, and academic freedom. This represents significant pushback against what critics call a compulsory opt-in culture where universities sign multimillion dollar deals with tech companies without clear evidence of educational benefits.

-

And from our Case Study category, Washington University in St. Louis has launched a universitywide academic initiative called Plus A.I. Led by Provost Mark West, the program aims to integrate artificial intelligence thoughtfully into teaching, learning, and research. It includes an A.I. literacy module for undergraduates, new generative A.I. tools, and faculty curriculum support. The initiative strives to balance A.I.'s potential with commitments to student formation and knowledge development.

-

Now, let's get back to that story I mentioned at the top about students demanding A.I. transparency at Missouri.

At the University of Missouri, something interesting is happening that flips the usual narrative about A.I. resistance in higher education. A student organization called Students for Human Intelligence has been systematically emailing professors across campus with a straightforward question: How do you plan to implement A.I. in your classes?

The group wants transparency so students can make informed decisions about which courses to take. They're not asking professors to stop using A.I. entirely, but they want to know what they're signing up for when they register for a class. In response to this student pressure, the university's Faculty Council is now voting on a proposed A.I. policy that would require instructors to disclose their level of A.I. usage using a standardized scale.

This represents a fascinating shift in campus A.I. conversations. For the past two years, most discussions have centered on preventing student misuse of A.I. tools. Institutions have been crafting honor codes, updating academic integrity policies, and training faculty to detect A.I.-generated work. Now we're seeing students themselves organizing to question faculty use of A.I. in instruction and curriculum design.

The Missouri situation highlights competing perspectives. Students for Human Intelligence argues that extensive A.I. use could devalue their education and that it's better to keep things human. Meanwhile, faculty committee chair Kevin Brown frames the proposed disclosure system as being proactive and responsive to student needs.

What makes this particularly complex is the practical challenge it creates. Most faculty members are still figuring out how to thoughtfully integrate A.I. tools into their teaching. Being required to categorize and publicly disclose their A.I. usage level adds a layer of complexity that many weren't anticipating. It also raises questions about what constitutes A.I. use in instruction. Does using ChatGPT to brainstorm discussion questions count the same as having students analyze A.I.-generated content?

The Missouri approach involves creating a tiered disclosure system where faculty would indicate their level of A.I. integration. But this surfaces deeper questions about academic freedom and pedagogical choice. When students can effectively vote with their feet by avoiding courses with higher A.I. usage ratings, it creates market pressures that could influence curricular decisions in unexpected ways.

For community colleges, where we serve diverse student populations with varying comfort levels around technology, this kind of transparency demand could be particularly complex to navigate. Many of our students are already juggling work, family, and financial pressures. The challenge for institutions is creating systems that honor student preferences while maintaining the pedagogical freedom faculty need to innovate.

-

The Missouri story surfaces a tension worth sitting with: transparency and academic freedom don't always align neatly. Finding the balance is the work ahead.

That's your Innovation Pulse for Monday. Find full coverage and links at innovating higher ed dot com. See you Tuesday.

At the University of Missouri, a student organization called Students for Human Intelligence has been emailing professors across campus asking how they plan to implement A.I. in their classes. Now we're seeing students themselves pushing for transparency about faculty use of A.I. in instruction and curriculum design. It's a reversal that catches many administrators off guard.

The Missouri situation highlights competing perspectives about A.I.'s role in education. Students for Human Intelligence argues that extensive A.I. use could "devalue all of our education" and that it's better to "keep things human." Meanwhile, faculty committee chair Kevin Brown frames the proposed disclosure system as being "proactive" and responsive to student needs while helping students "understand that we are listening to them."

What makes this particularly interesting is the practical challenge it creates for institutions. Most faculty members are still figuring out how to thoughtfully integrate A.I. tools into their teaching. Being required to categorize and publicly disclose their A.I. usage level adds a layer of complexity that many weren't anticipating. It also raises questions about what constitutes "A.I. use" in instruction — does using ChatGPT to brainstorm discussion questions count the same as having students analyze A.I.-generated content?

The Missouri approach — creating a tiered disclosure system — represents one institutional response to student demands for transparency. But it also surfaces deeper questions about academic freedom, pedagogical choice, and who gets to determine appropriate levels of A.I. integration. When students can effectively vote with their feet by avoiding courses with higher A.I. usage ratings, it creates market pressures that could influence curricular decisions in ways we haven't fully considered.

For those of us teaching Monday morning, this story matters because it suggests student attitudes about A.I. in education are more nuanced and varied than we might assume. Some students clearly want the option to choose courses with minimal A.I. integration. Others may be comfortable with or even prefer more A.I.-enhanced instruction. The challenge for institutions is creating systems that honor these preferences while maintaining academic integrity and pedagogical innovation.
